common_name: David's Lavender Phlox (Lavender Sport of David with White Starburst Eye)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; this lavender-flowered sport arose from the mildew-resistant white cultivar 'David' and inherited much of its disease tolerance.

directions: David's Lavender produces large, densely packed panicles of fragrant lavender-pink flowers, each marked with a small white starburst at the center, opening from midsummer into early fall. As a naturally occurring sport of the famous mildew-resistant 'David', it carries noticeably cleaner foliage through the humid months than most older tall garden phlox. Grow it in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil with generous spacing between clumps to keep air moving through the foliage. Deadheading spent flower heads encourages continued bloom and prevents unwanted self-sown seedlings, which do not come true to the parent color.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Orange Perfection Phlox (Salmon-Orange Red-Eyed Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moderately fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun; good air circulation between plants keeps this mildew-resistant selection performing well through the humid summer months.

directions: Orange Perfection stands out among tall garden phlox for its unusual salmon-orange flower color, each bloom accented by a deeper red eye, carried in dense rounded heads from midsummer through late summer. It is noted for stronger-than-average resistance to powdery mildew compared with older orange- and salmon-toned cultivars, keeping its narrow dark-green leaves attractive later into the season. Site it in full sun with fertile, medium-moisture soil and enough spacing for airflow, since crowded plantings are more prone to fungal leaf spot. The nectar-rich flowers are a strong draw for bees, hummingbirds, and butterflies and hold up well as cut flowers.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Lord Clayton Phlox (Scarlet-Red Garden Phlox with Purple-Bronze Foliage)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in compost-enriched, well-drained soil in full sun with good air circulation; the tinted foliage of this patented selection is most vivid in strong sun.

directions: Lord Clayton pairs deep scarlet-red flower clusters with distinctive foliage that emerges eggplant-purple with lime-green veins in spring before maturing to a bronzy purple-green through summer, giving it garden interest even before bloom. Flowering runs nearly continuously from late spring into late summer in a mildew-resistant, more compact habit than many older red-flowered garden phlox. Plant it in full sun in rich, well-drained soil with room around each clump for airflow, which helps preserve the colored foliage and limit fungal leaf disease. Its dark leaves make an effective color foil for silver- or gray-foliaged neighbors and ornamental grasses.

common_name: Party Girl Garden Phlox (White with Pink Star-Center, Garden Girls Series)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this Garden Girls series selection is bred for strong disease resistance and dependable rebloom.

directions: Party Girl carries large, fragrant white flower panicles, each floret marked with a small star-shaped light-pink center, on a compact, upright plant bred as part of the disease-resistant Garden Girls series. Unlike many older white garden phlox, it reblooms steadily after its main midsummer flush if lightly deadheaded, extending color into late summer. Grow it in full sun in fertile soil with consistent moisture and enough spacing for airflow to keep the dark-green foliage clean of powdery mildew. Its fragrance and rebloom habit make it a strong performer for cutting gardens and pollinator borders alike.

common_name: Dream Girl Garden Phlox (Lavender-Pink White-Eyed, Garden Girls Series)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part sun; Dream Girl blooms slightly later than most tall garden phlox and continues with strong rebloom.

directions: Dream Girl bears bright lavender-pink flowers with a crisp white eye on a vigorous, densely branched, vase-shaped plant that is part of the disease-resistant Garden Girls breeding line. It flowers a little later in the season than many older cultivars but compensates with excellent rebloom once the first flush fades, keeping color going into late summer. Plant it in full to part sun in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil, spacing plants generously to reduce powdery mildew pressure. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit the flowers heavily, making it a good choice for pollinator-focused perennial borders.

common_name: Sherbet Cocktail Phlox (Pink-and-Pale-Yellow Bicolor Garden Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this tall, late-blooming selection benefits from staking or interplanting with sturdy neighbors in windy sites.

directions: Sherbet Cocktail is a tall, strongly upright garden phlox notable for an unusual multi-tone flower color, with petals blending soft pink and pale greenish-yellow so each floret and each cluster looks subtly different. Buds open nearly yellow before shifting toward pink as the flowers mature, and bloom comes later in the season than most tall garden phlox, extending the display into early fall. Grow it in full sun in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil, giving the tall stems enough spacing for airflow since good mildew resistance is a hallmark of this selection. Hummingbirds and butterflies are frequent visitors to the long-lasting flower heads.

common_name: Cotton Candy Garden Phlox (Compact Pink Phlox with Orange Center Halo)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moderately fertile, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun; the compact habit of this patented selection suits containers and small border spaces.

directions: Cotton Candy is a compact, well-branched garden phlox bearing star-shaped flowers that blend lavender, soft pink, and white tones around a distinctive orange-tinted center halo. Its shorter stature compared with traditional tall garden phlox makes it well suited to containers, courtyard plantings, and the front-to-middle of a mixed border. Grow it in full sun to very light shade in moderately fertile, medium-moisture, well-drained soil, with enough spacing between plants for airflow to help maintain its noted mildew resistance. The fragrant flowers bloom from midsummer into early fall and draw hummingbirds and butterflies steadily through that period.
